input.body:
# 2028 Health-Benefits Tracker

## Elected medical plan

- **Exact recorded plan name:** Helio 2028 Employee-Only HDHP
- **Coverage period:** January 1, 2028–December 31, 2028
- **Status on January 1, 2028:** Elected; coverage began January 1, 2028

## Plan terms

- **Medical payroll deduction:** $98 per paycheck × 24 paychecks = **$2,352 expected annual medical premiums**
- **Employee HSA payroll election:** $125 per paycheck × 24 paychecks = **$3,000 expected annual employee HSA contributions**
- **Deductible:** $2,000
- **Out-of-pocket maximum:** $4,000

## Employer HSA deposits

Each deposit is **$250** and is contingent on remaining HSA-eligible on the applicable deposit date. These are separate from employee payroll deductions and should not be treated as funded until posted.

| Scheduled date | Expected amount | Eligibility condition | Actual amount posted | Posted date | Reconciled? |
|---|---:|---|---:|---|---|
| January 15, 2028 | $250 | HSA-eligible on January 15 | $_____ | __________ | ☐ |
| April 15, 2028 | $250 | HSA-eligible on April 15 | $_____ | __________ | ☐ |
| July 15, 2028 | $250 | HSA-eligible on July 15 | $_____ | __________ | ☐ |
| October 15, 2028 | $250 | HSA-eligible on October 15 | $_____ | __________ | ☐ |
| **Expected total** | **$1,000** | Eligibility required at each date | **$_____ actual total** |  |  |

## Year-end reconciliation

| Item | Expected 2028 amount | Actual 2028 amount | Difference | Verification source/notes |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| Medical premiums deducted | $2,352 | $_____ | $_____ | ______________________________ |
| Employee HSA contributions | $3,000 | $_____ | $_____ | ______________________________ |
| Employer HSA deposits | $1,000 if all four deposits occur | $_____ | $_____ | ______________________________ |
| **Combined HSA funding** | **$4,000 if all four deposits occur** | **$_____** | **$_____** | ______________________________ |

## Year-end checks

- ☐ Confirm 24 medical payroll deductions of $98 each.
- ☐ Confirm 24 employee HSA payroll deductions of $125 each.
- ☐ Reconcile each employer HSA deposit against the HSA portal and eligibility status on its scheduled date.
- ☐ Record any missed, reduced, delayed, or reversed employer deposit.
- ☐ Save year-end payroll and HSA statements.
- ☐ Record the final actual totals and explain any variance from expected amounts.

**Year-end reconciliation completed on:** ____________________

**Additional notes:**

__________________________________________________________________

input.title: July 26, 2024 roasted-chicken repeat test log
input.body:
# Dated test-log entry

**Run date:** July 26, 2024
**Product:** Roasted chicken
**Case and method:** Unchanged 30-pound case; tested pre-staging and tray sequence

## Threshold assessment

- **Incremental-labor threshold:** Met — 59 minutes used against a maximum of 60 minutes.
- **Yield threshold:** Met — 44 complete seven-ounce portions produced against a minimum of 44.

## Production and sell-through

- **Complete portions produced:** 44
- **Plates prepared:** 44
- **Plates sold:** 40
- **Unsold portions:** 4, handled under the restaurant’s approved staff-meal procedure
- **Sell-through:** 40 of 44, or 90.9%

## Demand comparison with the prior run

The June 28 run prepared 45 portions and sold 43, for 95.6% sell-through. The July 26 repeat sold 3 fewer portions and had sell-through 4.7 percentage points lower. Production met both controls, but demand was weaker than on the prior run.

input.title: Method card — 2024 Helio Start authority diagnostic
input.body:
# Method card — 2024 Helio Start authority diagnostic

**Use:** Historical reference for the narrow 2024 Helio Start diagnostic. This card describes the method and boundaries used then; it is not a current operating policy or a recommendation to change live processes.

## 1. Diagnostic question

Test whether post-admission support effort could be better understood by separating customer-side external access or authority blocks from product-guidance needs. The diagnostic was descriptive and mechanism-level, not an onboarding rebuild or a readiness-policy redesign.

## 2. Enrollment setup and window

- **Enrollment window:** October 1–28, 2024.
- **Cohort:** The first 60 qualifying workspaces admitted during that window.
- **Cohort close:** Enrollment stopped at the 60th qualifying workspace. HST-1060 was the 60th, admitted at 8:17 a.m. on October 25; HST-1061, admitted at 8:42 a.m., remained outside the diagnostic.
- **Later admissions:** Stayed outside the diagnostic, with their live routing unchanged.
- **Design:** Prospective classification after admission, with evidence recorded as cases unfolded.
- **Operating state:** Admission, pending-state, and assisted-routing rules remained unchanged throughout. Diagnostic classification was not a live eligibility or routing decision.

## 3. Prospective classification categories

Classify each enrolled workspace prospectively as:

1. **External access or authority** — the remaining blocker depended on customer-side control, permission, ownership, security approval, network allowlisting, or another external system authority.
2. **Product guidance** — the blocker was help understanding or completing a Helio/product setup step when the required external access or authority was available.
3. **Mixed** — both an external access or authority blocker and a product-guidance need materially contributed to the case.

Keep these dimensions distinct when interpreting a case:

- Helio admin proof;
- connector authentication; and
- authority in the external system.

Passing Helio admin-proof and connector-authentication checks did not establish that the customer had the external authority needed to complete setup.

## 4. Tracked support outcomes

For each enrolled workspace with support activity, track:

- **Resolution time**, using the diagnostic’s stated business-day convention;
- **Substantive repeat contacts**, excluding automated acknowledgements and counting a repeat only when a customer or agent added a new substantive contact after the initial case entry;
- **Summed human agent-minutes**, the active work performed by human agents;
- **Elapsed customer-blocked time**, retained separately from human agent-minutes rather than substituted for them; and
- **Prospective category**: external access or authority, product guidance, or mixed.

The final 2024 closeout recorded 17 support-contacting workspaces and 486 post-admission human agent-minutes among the 60 enrolled workspaces:

- Seven external access or authority cases: 301 minutes, 3.6-business-day median resolution, and 12 substantive repeat contacts;
- Ten product-guidance cases: 185 minutes, 1.4-day median resolution, and six substantive repeat contacts; and
- No final mixed case was reported in the closeout totals.

All authority cases had already passed Helio admin-proof and connector-authentication checks. This supported the interpretation that external-system authority was a separate readiness input, not a synonym for either of those checks.

## 5. Completion and close rule

The diagnostic could close on December 12, 2024 only if the cohort reached 60 qualifying workspaces by October 28. If it had not reached 60 by that cutoff, close would wait until every enrolled workspace had a complete 45-day support window.

The cohort did reach 60 by October 25, and all 60 workspaces ultimately completed their 45-day support windows. The final close therefore occurred on December 12, 2024.

## 6. What the original eight cases justified

The original eight high-effort workspaces justified a bounded historical diagnostic to test the mechanism-level distinction between customer-side authority blocks and product guidance. They supported:

- retaining the accepted 52-workspace cohort and its day-90 statuses as context;
- excluding pre-admission connector assistance and billing contacts from the support-effort analysis;
- defining a prospective first-60-workspace diagnostic;
- using named categories and explicit support measures; and
- preserving a descriptive interpretation until the diagnostic’s completion rule was met.

They did **not** establish incidence for all applicants, a causal explanation of onboarding performance, or a basis for broad operational redesign.

## 7. What the original eight cases did not justify

Historically, the original eight cases did not justify:

- changing Helio Start intake or adding an owner-availability question;
- changing admission, pending-state, eligibility, or assisted-routing rules;
- changing lifecycle emails or suppression behavior;
- adding staffing or support capacity;
- rebuilding onboarding broadly;
- making CAC, paid-channel, pipeline, forecast, revenue, or conversion claims; or
- treating external authority as a new live readiness label without a separate approved decision.

The diagnostic’s later evidence likewise remained bounded: its prospective classifications and support outcomes did not retroactively convert the diagnostic into a live admission or routing policy.

## 8. Reuse guardrail

When reusing this method, label every conclusion as historical to the 2024 diagnostic unless a new design is explicitly approved. Preserve the separation between evidence collection and operating change; do not infer that a support category, early rate, or small cohort result authorizes intake, lifecycle, routing, staffing, or acquisition changes.

input.title: Helio Start field-handling quick reference
input.body:
# Helio Start field-handling quick reference

## Keep these states separate

- **Helio admin proof:** confirms the required Helio administrator evidence. It is not external-system authority.
- **Connector authentication:** confirms authentication to the selected connector. It is not proof that an owner can perform a required external action.
- **Entitlement and billing:** remain their own eligibility fields; neither establishes external authority.
- **External-system authority:** records whether the account or an available owner can perform the selected connector’s required owner-level permission or network-allowlist action. It is connector-readiness state—not consent, contact permission, message eligibility, or proof that the integration is live.
- **Messaging state:** remains governed separately. Verified external authority does not authorize automated contact or setup messaging by itself.

## State handling

- **Verified:** external authority is current and verified; it may support the applicable connector-readiness and admission flow, subject to all other current checks.
- **Pending, missing, stale, unresolved, conflicting, no, or not sure:** fail closed or use the established assisted route. Preserve the field-specific reason, keep the applicant pending before admission where applicable, and withhold setup prompts. Do not relabel the state as a connector-authentication failure or final ineligibility.

## Ownership

- **Daniela** records external-authority readiness as a separate state.
- **Ines** holds setup prompts and related setup messaging while that state is pending; she does not treat verified authority as blanket permission to contact.
- **Owen** reports external-authority state separately from the other admission, lifecycle, and messaging measures.

Existing admin-proof, connector-authentication, entitlement, billing, deployment, admission, routing, and messaging rules remain unchanged.

input.title: Current Authority Reference — Routine CS Auto-Nudge Messaging-State Reviews
input.body:
# Current authority reference

**Effective as of:** January 1, 2028  
**Scope:** Routine Customer Success (CS) auto-nudge messaging-state reviews and related routine operator guidance only.

## Ines may close without line-by-line approval

Ines may independently close a review and own the related routine operator guidance when **all** of the following are true:

- All five governed fields retain their established meanings and have current, consistent state:
  - external-system authority;
  - connector authentication;
  - entitlement;
  - qualifying-human-admin status; and
  - active Customer Success adoption or renewal work.
- The messaging view and nudge view agree.
- The decision is routine and non-state-changing.
- There is no customer-correction, incident-stop, ambiguity, exception-heavy condition, disputed semantics, disputed interpretation, cross-surface consequence, or executive-claim issue.

No line-by-line approval from Riley is required for a review that satisfies these conditions. A proceed result is not blanket permission for automated contact: external-system authority means connector readiness for the required owner-level permission or network-allowlist action.

## Required handling of holds and suppressions

- **Current active Customer Success adoption or renewal work:** suppresses the nudge under the shared contract; it is not an Ines discretion call.
- **Missing, stale, unresolved, or conflicting required state:** fails closed as a visible, field-specific hold. Do not manually release the nudge or a dependent lifecycle message. Require a fresh source check and system reevaluation.
- Owen retains the routine exception ledger and routine operating explanation. Source, transport, reliability, release, and rollback issues remain with Daniela as applicable.

## Escalate to Riley immediately

Escalate rather than close in Ines’s routine lane when the review involves any of the following:

- a customer correction or incident stop;
- a state-changing send or decision;
- ambiguous or disputed semantics, interpretations, or field meanings;
- an exception-heavy case or cross-surface consequence; or
- an executive claim or other final operating claim.

Keep the affected decision held while the issue is resolved. Stale, unresolved, or conflicting state is not a reason to waive the hold; it remains failed closed pending fresh evidence and reevaluation.

## Work outside Ines’s authority

This decision does **not** give Ines closure authority over:

- Helio Start reporting;
- Expansion Assist selection;
- lifecycle preflight;
- lifecycle-send release limits or other lifecycle release authority;
- any additional consumer or a fifth consumer; or
- any scope beyond the existing four production consumers.

It also does not grant Ines engineering release, transport, source-reliability, or rollback control. Daniela retains those engineering controls. Riley retains the listed exception, semantic, cross-surface, customer-correction, incident-stop, state-changing, ambiguous, exception-heavy, and executive-claim authority. The four-consumer scope and all established authority lanes remain unchanged.

input.title: Q4 Pricing Path Clarity Test — Outcome Memo
input.body:
# Q4 Pricing Path Clarity Test — Outcome Memo

**Status:** Certified four-cohort result; organic rollout completed November 26, 2025.

## Outcome

Across 3,286 organic pricing-page sessions—1,639 control and 1,647 treatment—Owen’s certified read showed fewer Helio Start eligibility-flow starts later routed out for an existing unsupported condition:

- **Control:** 38 of 344 starts, or 11.0%
- **Treatment:** 25 of 352 starts, or 7.1%
- **Result:** 35.7% relative reduction

The direction held across all three weekly cohorts and the November 10–16 stabilization cohort, with no unrelated pricing-page layout or UI change.

## Threshold and guardrails

- **Predeclared path-quality threshold — PASSED:** at least a 25% relative reduction was required; observed reduction was **35.7%**.
- **Eligible-workspace admission completion guardrail — PASSED:** no more than a 1.5-percentage-point decline was allowed; control was **43.8%** versus treatment at **44.1%**—a **0.3-point improvement**, not a decline.
- **Account-level support-time guardrail at the 90th percentile — PASSED:** no more than a 10-minute increase was allowed; control was **71 minutes** versus treatment at **74 minutes**, a **3-minute increase**.

## Rollout supported

The result supports adopting the path-separated design for **organic pricing-page traffic**: bounded under-50, simple-deployment Helio Start needs receive a separate entry path from assisted needs. Priya approved the design, Daniela moved treatment to **100% of organic traffic on November 26, 2025**, and the control was retired.

## Boundaries unchanged

The rollout does not change existing:

- Helio Start eligibility or refusal rules
- Connector-access or external-authority requirements
- Lifecycle branches
- Instrumentation and event taxonomy
- Customer Success and assisted support-routing rules
- Paid-acquisition scope or traffic treatment
- Pipeline definitions or targets
- Forecast-credit rules

## Commercial conclusions not established

This result supports a narrow claim about **fewer unsupported self-serve starts and the organic pricing-page rollout decision**. It does **not** establish:

- Revenue lift or improved monetization
- Paid-acquisition economics or broader acquisition impact
- Pipeline impact or pipeline causality
- Forecast performance or forecast credit
- A change in Helio Start eligibility, admission policy, or refusal policy
- A causal claim about outcomes outside the tested path-quality metric and predeclared guardrails

**Claim-safe conclusion:** The path-separated organic pricing-page experience cleared its predeclared path-quality threshold and both guardrails, supporting its rollout to organic traffic while leaving all admission, lifecycle, support-routing, acquisition, pipeline, and forecast boundaries intact.

input.title: Private Portfolio Entry — Cherrywood Kitchen-Window Studies (August 2027)
input.body:
# Cherrywood Kitchen-Window Studies

- **Session:** Private two-person watercolor session with Mom during her August 1–7, 2027 Cherrywood visit.
- **Date and time:** August 7, 2027, 9:00am–11:00am.
- **Subject:** The same Cherrywood kitchen-window setup.
- **Materials and format:** Riley’s watercolor supplies; two separate studies, each 9 × 12 inches.

## Studies

- **Riley’s study:** 9 × 12 inches; fully dry; placed in Riley’s private watercolor portfolio at Cherrywood.
- **Mom’s study:** 9 × 12 inches; fully dry; taken by Mom when Riley handled her scheduled 4:20pm AUS departure back to Sacramento.

## Commitments

Neither study has a sale, exhibition, or public-demonstration commitment. The session remained private and created no additional public or commercial obligation.

input.title: Historical decision note — April 21, 2023 staff review
input.body:
## Decision

The leading hypothesis remained supported, but the churn issue was not yet considered fixed. The team would not close the investigation or make a definitive claim from the current chart alone.

## Evidence still required

A clean third stabilization cohort was required to show that the improvement held under normal operating conditions. The April 21 review also recorded that the weaker second cohort appeared to reflect a one-off Customer Success outage, not evidence that the fix itself had failed; the cohort-3 result was therefore needed to confirm the distinction.

## Expected timing

The third cohort was expected the following week, in the week of April 24, 2023. The conclusion remained conditional on that cohort holding.

input.title: Helio Start archive note — origins, workstreams, and guardrails
input.body:
# Helio Start archive note

## Purpose

For onboarding and retrospective use. This note records how the original sub-50-seat effort was framed, what it covered, and why commercial decisions were kept distinct from eligibility and product constraints.

## Original duration

- **Initial scoping:** 10 days, with the scoping doc due May 26.
- **Subsequent implementation estimate:** 12 weeks to establish the required operating-model foundations. This was not treated as a fast pricing toggle.

The 10-day commitment was for deciding what had to be true and what the team would refuse or route elsewhere. The 12-week estimate covered the underlying work needed across instrumentation, product boundaries, lifecycle, support, and related operating paths.

## Core workstreams

1. **Eligibility and refusal rules**
   - Define eligibility using deployment shape and admin complexity, not seat count alone.
   - Establish explicit boundaries for seat caps, workspace limits, permissions, billing exceptions, import/migration needs, admin ownership, and access to human help.
   - Separate customer-protective refusal or assisted-routing rules from judgments about whether small accounts are valuable.

2. **Entitlement, event taxonomy, and measurement**
   - Rework funnel and entitlement instrumentation so the team could observe admin complexity, import or migration help, support handoffs, and entitlement state.
   - Use activation definition v3 for the sub-50 analysis, while keeping the 75–200-seat retained mid-segment comparison separate and showing the 50–75-seat band separately.
   - Treat the baseline as descriptive evidence for eligibility and operating-model decisions, not as proof that seat count alone determines success.

3. **Onboarding, lifecycle, and support paths**
   - Map where self-serve onboarding would need to fork for ordinary setup versus cases requiring documentation, assisted routing, or refusal.
   - Identify support-load risks before promising a self-serve experience.
   - Avoid state-changing lifecycle automation until eligibility and routing states were clear.

4. **Commercial and pricing-page constraints**
   - Evaluate packaging, seat caps, feature fences, billing behavior, and any sales-assist rules separately from the product and eligibility analysis.
   - Keep pricing-page work behind the instrumentation and operating-model gates, including the no-concurrent-layout-change rule.
   - Do not treat public pricing-page copy, a cheap-plan promise, or a Q3 launch implication as part of the initial scoping decision.

## How the guardrails related

The commercial guardrails were a containment layer, not a substitute for product readiness. Packaging or lower pricing could not by itself solve unsupported permissions, unclear workspace ownership, complex billing, import or migration work, or an onboarding path that required human troubleshooting.

Accordingly, the effort was split into two related but distinct questions:

- **Commercial guardrails:** What could be described, priced, or exposed without creating an accidental public promise or changing unrelated pricing surfaces?
- **Eligibility and product constraints:** Which account and deployment shapes could safely use the intended path, and where should the experience refuse, route to assistance, or remain unsupported?

The intended sequence was to establish eligibility, refusal, entitlement, lifecycle, and support boundaries first; then use the evidence to inform any later commercial or pricing-page decision. The working name “Helio Start” referred to the internal sub-50-seat motion and scenario exploration, not an automatic launch commitment.

## Retrospective takeaway

The original effort was an operating-model and readiness exercise, not a pricing-only project. The durable lesson is to keep seat count from becoming a proxy for eligibility: commercial packaging can frame an offer, but deployment shape, admin complexity, entitlement behavior, lifecycle handling, and support capacity determine whether that offer can be delivered safely.

observed.body:
# Helio Start archive note

## Purpose

For onboarding and retrospective use. This note records how the original sub-50-seat effort was framed, what it covered, and why commercial decisions were kept distinct from eligibility and product constraints.

## Original duration

- **Initial scoping:** 10 days, with the scoping doc due May 26.
- **Subsequent implementation estimate:** 12 weeks to establish the required operating-model foundations. This was not treated as a fast pricing toggle.

The 10-day commitment was for deciding what had to be true and what the team would refuse or route elsewhere. The 12-week estimate covered the underlying work needed across instrumentation, product boundaries, lifecycle, support, and related operating paths.

## Core workstreams

1. **Eligibility and refusal rules**
   - Define eligibility using deployment shape and admin complexity, not seat count alone.
   - Establish explicit boundaries for seat caps, workspace limits, permissions, billing exceptions, import/migration needs, admin ownership, and access to human help.
   - Separate customer-protective refusal or assisted-routing rules from judgments about whether small accounts are valuable.

2. **Entitlement, event taxonomy, and measurement**
   - Rework funnel and entitlement instrumentation so the team could observe admin complexity, import or migration help, support handoffs, and entitlement state.
   - Use activation definition v3 for the sub-50 analysis, while keeping the 75–200-seat retained mid-segment comparison separate and showing the 50–75-seat band separately.
   - Treat the baseline as descriptive evidence for eligibility and operating-model decisions, not as proof that seat count alone determines success.

3. **Onboarding, lifecycle, and support paths**
   - Map where self-serve onboarding would need to fork for ordinary setup versus cases requiring documentation, assisted routing, or refusal.
   - Identify support-load risks before promising a self-serve experience.
   - Avoid state-changing lifecycle automation until eligibility and routing states were clear.

4. **Commercial and pricing-page constraints**
   - Evaluate packaging, seat caps, feature fences, billing behavior, and any sales-assist rules separately from the product and eligibility analysis.
   - Keep pricing-page work behind the instrumentation and operating-model gates, including the no-concurrent-layout-change rule.
   - Do not treat public pricing-page copy, a cheap-plan promise, or a Q3 launch implication as part of the initial scoping decision.

## How the guardrails related

The commercial guardrails were a containment layer, not a substitute for product readiness. Packaging or lower pricing could not by itself solve unsupported permissions, unclear workspace ownership, complex billing, import or migration work, or an onboarding path that required human troubleshooting.

Accordingly, the effort was split into two related but distinct questions:

- **Commercial guardrails:** What could be described, priced, or exposed without creating an accidental public promise or changing unrelated pricing surfaces?
- **Eligibility and product constraints:** Which account and deployment shapes could safely use the intended path, and where should the experience refuse, route to assistance, or remain unsupported?

The intended sequence was to establish eligibility, refusal, entitlement, lifecycle, and support boundaries first; then use the evidence to inform any later commercial or pricing-page decision. The working name “Helio Start” referred to the internal sub-50-seat motion and scenario exploration, not an automatic launch commitment.

## Retrospective takeaway

The original effort was an operating-model and readiness exercise, not a pricing-only project. The durable lesson is to keep seat count from becoming a proxy for eligibility: commercial packaging can frame an offer, but deployment shape, admin complexity, entitlement behavior, lifecycle handling, and support capacity determine whether that offer can be delivered safely.

input.title: Helio Start lifecycle-design checklist
input.body:
# Helio Start lifecycle-design checklist

Use this checklist before approving any Helio Start lifecycle copy, audience, trigger, or automation.

## Required decision record

- [ ] **Lifecycle-fork choice recorded:** **Use the conservative Helio Start lifecycle fork.** Keep Helio Start separate from the retained-mid onboarding path; preserve the eligibility, refusal, support-routing, and admin-ownership boundaries.
- [ ] **Wholesale reuse decision recorded:** **Do not reuse the retained-mid onboarding and lifecycle path wholesale.** Its assumptions do not fit Helio Start: multi-admin invitations, sufficient integration-owner permission context, and upgrade/team-use language before simple self-serve workspaces understand imports and billing.
- [ ] The reviewer has recorded both approved answers above in the approval note. Neither item may remain an open choice or be described as “to be decided.”

## Copy and automation checks

- [ ] Copy is customer-protective and does not imply that lifecycle messaging solves migration help, CSV/import work, manual billing exceptions, complex permissions, unclear admin ownership, or heavy support needs.
- [ ] Those unsupported or assisted cases route out of the first self-serve motion through the approved path; they are not forced through a lifecycle edge case.
- [ ] Any touch is clearly educational or operationally appropriate for the conservative fork; it does not introduce premature upgrade, team-use, launch, or beta language.
- [ ] State-changing automation is not approved through proxy signals or guessed entitlement/support state. Missing, stale, unresolved, or conflicting state fails closed.
- [ ] Current-state suppression behavior and existing lifecycle branches are preserved; no paid-source bypass or new unsupported branch is created.
- [ ] The reviewer records whether the touch is non-state-changing education or state-changing automation, along with the applicable QA and approval gate.

## Final approval record

- [ ] Approved copy/version and audience or trigger are identified.
- [ ] Eligibility, entitlement, support-state, admin-ownership, and refusal-boundary evidence is current and complete.
- [ ] Owner, rollback/stop condition, and manual-review requirement are recorded where applicable.
- [ ] Approval explicitly confirms that the two required decisions above remain unchanged.

input.title: Investigation readout operating note
input.body:
## Standing practice

The investigation framework is the standing readout practice for Growth and Customer Success. Readouts should put the denominator and observed effect size before the conclusion, distinguish first significance from stabilization-cohort confirmation, and keep lifecycle audience risk in the review. First significance alone does not justify rollout; the result must stabilize before a ship decision.

## Ownership

Owen maintains the standard readout shape and examples. Ines maintains the lifecycle-risk portion and language.

## Limits

This is a lightweight team practice, not a companywide mandatory template. Teams may reuse the framework without routing every readout through Riley, Owen, or Ines. Owen’s and Ines’s lanes maintain the guidance and review boundaries; they are not approval requirements for every individual readout.

input.title: New Growth and Customer Success lifecycle decisioning — pre-design intake checklist
input.body:
# Purpose

Use this checklist before designing any new Growth or Customer Success lifecycle decisioning: eligibility, suppression, routing, handoff, hold, reminder, nudge, or message behavior.

## Hard prerequisite

The proposal must use the shared lifecycle state contract. The governed fields remain distinct and must retain their existing meanings:

- External authority
- Connector authentication
- Entitlement
- Qualifying-human-admin status
- Active Customer Success adoption or renewal work

Each required field must have one source owner, an as-of time, and a freshness limit. Missing, stale, or conflicting state must fail closed and map to a visible hold; do not reuse prior eligibility or infer a governed state from a proxy.

**May design proceed before this prerequisite is satisfied? No—not as an approved lifecycle-decisioning design.** Teams may document the problem, map the desired customer experience, and record missing inputs, but they must not finalize a new eligibility, suppression, routing, handoff, hold, or message rule until the shared-state contract is confirmed for the use case. No experiment, production change, or customer-facing decisioning may proceed on an ungoverned state.

## Intake checklist

### 1. Decision and scope

- [ ] Name the Growth or Customer Success use case.
- [ ] State the customer action being considered.
- [ ] Identify the exact decision: display, suppress, hold, route, hand off, or do nothing.
- [ ] Define the intended surface and audience.
- [ ] State what is explicitly out of scope, including any reuse of this decision for other outreach.
- [ ] Confirm whether the work is exploratory design only or intended for later implementation. Do not describe exploratory work as live, approved, or production-ready.

### 2. Shared-state mapping

For every field used by the decision:

- [ ] Name the governed contract field; do not create a parallel meaning.
- [ ] Record the source owner.
- [ ] Record the as-of time and freshness limit.
- [ ] Define the valid states, including missing, stale, conflicting, pending, and unknown where applicable.
- [ ] Explain how the decision behaves for each invalid or unavailable state.
- [ ] Confirm that eligibility, reporting, and messaging will read the same governed state.
- [ ] Confirm that no connector choice, signup age, seat count, usage signal, or other proxy is being used as a substitute for a governed field.

### 3. Decision rules and holds

- [ ] Write the positive eligibility condition in plain language.
- [ ] Write every suppression condition, especially active Customer Success adoption or renewal work when relevant.
- [ ] Write the visible hold condition for missing, stale, unresolved, or conflicting required state.
- [ ] Define reevaluation timing and require fresh evaluation for each possible display or action.
- [ ] State whether a proceed result is limited to this use case; it does not create blanket contact permission or a reusable audience.
- [ ] Define the fail-closed behavior and the human-readable reason shown to operators where applicable.

### 4. Ownership and operational path

- [ ] Identify the decision owner and customer-correction owner.
- [ ] Identify the reporting owner for denominator, exceptions, and outcome interpretation.
- [ ] Identify the messaging owner for state consumption and copy treatment.
- [ ] Identify the engineering owner for transport, source reliability, release, and rollback.
- [ ] Define the Customer Success handoff trigger, transferred context, response expectation, after-hours treatment, and escalation path if a handoff is part of the design.
- [ ] Preserve account-level support time from first contact; do not reset the clock at handoff.

### 5. Measurement and safety boundaries

- [ ] Define the denominator and the exact event or state that will be measured.
- [ ] Keep activation, conversion, retention, revenue, pipeline, support load, and forecast claims separate.
- [ ] Define holdout or comparison requirements before making a causal claim.
- [ ] List monitoring for source age, held records, conflicting records, display counts, routing failures, and suppression failures.
- [ ] Define the incident stop owner and rollback owner.
- [ ] Confirm that the design does not authorize budget, paid traffic, a batch, pipeline treatment, forecast credit, launch, or production release by itself.

## Intake decision

- **Proceed to design review:** the shared-state contract is confirmed for every required field and all checklist items are complete or explicitly assigned as non-blocking design follow-up.
- **Return for contract work:** any required field lacks a source owner, freshness limit, settled meaning, or fail-closed behavior.
- **Hold:** any proposal relies on missing, stale, conflicting, or reused prior state, or attempts to turn a proceed result into permission for another use case.

Completion of this checklist is an intake and design-control record. It is not approval to launch, send, experiment, spend, create a paid audience, claim revenue, or alter production behavior.

observed.body:
# Purpose

Use this checklist before designing any new Growth or Customer Success lifecycle decisioning: eligibility, suppression, routing, handoff, hold, reminder, nudge, or message behavior.

## Hard prerequisite

The proposal must use the shared lifecycle state contract. The governed fields remain distinct and must retain their existing meanings:

- External authority
- Connector authentication
- Entitlement
- Qualifying-human-admin status
- Active Customer Success adoption or renewal work

Each required field must have one source owner, an as-of time, and a freshness limit. Missing, stale, or conflicting state must fail closed and map to a visible hold; do not reuse prior eligibility or infer a governed state from a proxy.

**May design proceed before this prerequisite is satisfied? No—not as an approved lifecycle-decisioning design.** Teams may document the problem, map the desired customer experience, and record missing inputs, but they must not finalize a new eligibility, suppression, routing, handoff, hold, or message rule until the shared-state contract is confirmed for the use case. No experiment, production change, or customer-facing decisioning may proceed on an ungoverned state.

## Intake checklist

### 1. Decision and scope

- [ ] Name the Growth or Customer Success use case.
- [ ] State the customer action being considered.
- [ ] Identify the exact decision: display, suppress, hold, route, hand off, or do nothing.
- [ ] Define the intended surface and audience.
- [ ] State what is explicitly out of scope, including any reuse of this decision for other outreach.
- [ ] Confirm whether the work is exploratory design only or intended for later implementation. Do not describe exploratory work as live, approved, or production-ready.

### 2. Shared-state mapping

For every field used by the decision:

- [ ] Name the governed contract field; do not create a parallel meaning.
- [ ] Record the source owner.
- [ ] Record the as-of time and freshness limit.
- [ ] Define the valid states, including missing, stale, conflicting, pending, and unknown where applicable.
- [ ] Explain how the decision behaves for each invalid or unavailable state.
- [ ] Confirm that eligibility, reporting, and messaging will read the same governed state.
- [ ] Confirm that no connector choice, signup age, seat count, usage signal, or other proxy is being used as a substitute for a governed field.

### 3. Decision rules and holds

- [ ] Write the positive eligibility condition in plain language.
- [ ] Write every suppression condition, especially active Customer Success adoption or renewal work when relevant.
- [ ] Write the visible hold condition for missing, stale, unresolved, or conflicting required state.
- [ ] Define reevaluation timing and require fresh evaluation for each possible display or action.
- [ ] State whether a proceed result is limited to this use case; it does not create blanket contact permission or a reusable audience.
- [ ] Define the fail-closed behavior and the human-readable reason shown to operators where applicable.

### 4. Ownership and operational path

- [ ] Identify the decision owner and customer-correction owner.
- [ ] Identify the reporting owner for denominator, exceptions, and outcome interpretation.
- [ ] Identify the messaging owner for state consumption and copy treatment.
- [ ] Identify the engineering owner for transport, source reliability, release, and rollback.
- [ ] Define the Customer Success handoff trigger, transferred context, response expectation, after-hours treatment, and escalation path if a handoff is part of the design.
- [ ] Preserve account-level support time from first contact; do not reset the clock at handoff.

### 5. Measurement and safety boundaries

- [ ] Define the denominator and the exact event or state that will be measured.
- [ ] Keep activation, conversion, retention, revenue, pipeline, support load, and forecast claims separate.
- [ ] Define holdout or comparison requirements before making a causal claim.
- [ ] List monitoring for source age, held records, conflicting records, display counts, routing failures, and suppression failures.
- [ ] Define the incident stop owner and rollback owner.
- [ ] Confirm that the design does not authorize budget, paid traffic, a batch, pipeline treatment, forecast credit, launch, or production release by itself.

## Intake decision

- **Proceed to design review:** the shared-state contract is confirmed for every required field and all checklist items are complete or explicitly assigned as non-blocking design follow-up.
- **Return for contract work:** any required field lacks a source owner, freshness limit, settled meaning, or fail-closed behavior.
- **Hold:** any proposal relies on missing, stale, conflicting, or reused prior state, or attempts to turn a proceed result into permission for another use case.

Completion of this checklist is an intake and design-control record. It is not approval to launch, send, experiment, spend, create a paid audience, claim revenue, or alter production behavior.

input.title: Cherrywood household maintenance — dishwasher (updated 2028-01-01)
input.body:
# Current status

The Cherrywood dishwasher is cleared for ordinary use as of January 1, 2028. No dishwasher-specific repair or follow-up is pending, and the earlier pump-failure no-use restriction has ended.

# Maintenance history

- **September 11, 2025:** After a normal cycle, the dishwasher stopped with standing water above the filter and produced a low hum on attempted restart. There was no reported floor leak, smoke, burning odor, breaker trip, or visible cabinet damage.
- **September 16, 2025:** Only the user-removable filter was removed and rinsed; no visible food or glass obstruction was found. No panels or pump components were disassembled. The dishwasher remained out of service pending maintenance.
- **September 23, 2025:** Cherrywood removed the standing water and diagnosed a failed drain pump. No user-removable obstruction, floor leak, electrical damage, cabinet damage, smoke, or burning odor was found. The replacement pump was ordered, so the dishwasher remained off limits.
- **October 1, 2025:** Cherrywood replaced the failed drain pump and successfully ran a full fill-and-drain cycle. The technician checked the appliance, floor, sink cabinet, and electrical connection and found no leak, electrical fault, smoke, burning odor, or cabinet damage. The dishwasher returned to ordinary service.
- **March 21, 2027:** A later cycle filled, washed, drained, and dried normally. Two glasses had a cloudy film, but there was no leak, cabinet moisture, electrical odor, smoke, unusual heat, or error indicator.
- **November 16, 2027:** After Cherrywood water service was restored, hot and cold flow were normal and the washer and dishwasher were cleared for ordinary use. No dishwasher issue or follow-up repair was reported.

# Precautions and next steps

No special dishwasher precautions currently apply: Riley and Sam do not need to keep it unused or follow the prior pump-failure precautions. Use it normally. If standing water, a leak, electrical odor or smoke, unusual heat, an error indicator, abnormal noise, or a drain backup returns, stop using it and contact Cherrywood maintenance rather than running repeated cycles or disassembling the pump area.

input.title: Standing investigation framework — ownership map
input.body:
# Purpose

Keep the standing investigation framework lightweight and maintained by the teams using it. This map routes framework-content updates without turning Riley into the reviewer for every readout or making the practice a companywide mandatory template.

## Ownership lanes

- **Owen — standard readout shape and examples:** Maintain the denominator, effect-size-before-conclusion, and conclusion-order guidance; update reusable examples and clarify the readout structure.
- **Ines — lifecycle-risk content:** Maintain lifecycle-risk language, audience-risk caveats, and lifecycle recommendation guidance. Keep the first-significance / stabilization-cohort boundary visible where lifecycle decisions are involved.
- **Riley — judgment and escalation:** Own decision rules, cross-functional tradeoffs, and escalations when a proposed change affects governed meaning, audience, owner boundaries, or executive language. Riley is not a routine approval step for framework edits or individual readouts.

## Routing rule

Send standard shape or example updates to Owen, and lifecycle-risk content to Ines. Teams may maintain and reuse the framework directly; involve Riley only for the escalation conditions above or for a cross-functional decision that the existing guidance does not resolve.

- Weekly active users: 41 three weeks ago; 35 two weeks ago; 26 this week.

- Primary champion: parental leave through June 3.

Assess which details are genuine risk signals versus temporary or ambiguous context. Then draft focused follow-up questions for Customer Success to test product engagement, interim ownership, and procurement timing rather than prematurely labeling the account a churn risk.

Draft intro:
`Conclusion: mid-segment teams who received the new setup reminder were less likely to churn, so the first significant read supports increasing lifecycle reminders in the renewal window.

Hypothesis: additional reminders improve engagement before renewal.

Metric/cohort/window: September renewal cohort, 75-200 seat accounts, churn within 30 days of renewal notice. Preliminary result is p<.05 with +0.7 points retained versus accounts that did not receive the reminder.

Proposed action: add a second reminder email for accounts that have not invited a teammate by day 10 of the renewal window.`

Riley's concern: conclusion appears before effect size; +0.7 points may be statistically significant but not necessarily decision-relevant; this is first significance rather than stabilization-cohort confirmation; the proposed lifecycle send needs a risk note before anyone turns the finding into another email.

input.title: PRE-RULING — Mid-segment churn investigation: H2 historical comparison phase
input.hypothesis: H2 — Seasonal / competitor-cycle explanation: the February mid-segment monthly-churn spike may reflect a recurring seasonal pattern or competitor activity rather than a change specific to the product, onboarding, or customer-success experience. This brief preserves the hypothesis as active and under test; it is not the later ruling.
input.metric_of_record: Monthly churn rate for the v1 mid-segment cohort: paid accounts with 50–200 seats. Signal at the time was 5.1% monthly churn versus a 2.1% trailing-six-month baseline.
input.cohort_scope: Pre-ruling v1 mid-segment definition: 50–200 seats, using the same cohort logic as the January scan and Owen’s independent recheck. Historical comparisons should use the same cut and denominator handling; do not substitute the later 75–200-seat v2 definition.
input.timeline: Historical pre-ruling phase, February 17–21, 2023. The planned H2 ruling was targeted for first thing on February 21, after the historical comparison work; this artifact intentionally stops before that ruling.
input.body:
STATUS — PRE-RULING ARTIFACT

Purpose
Capture the H2 investigation state before a conclusion was made. The 5.1% mid-segment monthly-churn signal had held after a second pass with Owen and Riley’s recheck, so the team was testing whether the spike was a recurring seasonal/competitor-cycle effect. No final H2 ruling belongs in this artifact.

Active hypothesis
H2: the observed mid-segment churn spike could be explained by seasonality, a competitor cycle, or timestamped competitor activity affecting the February window. The working standard was to test this against historical data before calling the period a “weird month.”

Planned historical-comparison work
1. Pull historical February comparisons before accepting a seasonal explanation.
2. Use the same cohort logic as the January scan and Owen’s check, keeping the 50–200-seat v1 cut and denominator treatment consistent.
3. Line up same-window monthly churn by segment, rather than relying on a total-company read.
4. Put the historical comparisons beside the current signal so the comparison is auditable.
5. Overlay obvious market dates and any competitor activity that can actually be timestamped.
6. Have Owen review or run the first pass where available, then preserve the cuts and rationale in the ruling record.

Investigation context
The working hypothesis stack was: H1 pricing artifact; H2 competitor cycle; H3 onboarding timing; H4 CS coverage gap. H1 had already been weakened by a tier split that came back essentially flat, but H2 remained an open explanation at this stage. The pricing-page experiment was kept as a separate parallel track and was not to be used as an explanation for this churn read or allowed to add noise to the investigation.

Ruling one-pager agreement
Owner: Owen writes one one-pager for every hypothesis ruling, whether the hypothesis is ruled in or ruled out. Riley owns the investigation document and its running chronology; that is separate from ownership of the ruling one-pagers.

Required contents for each one-pager:
• the rationale for the ruling;
• the exact cohort and analytical cuts used;
• p-value and effect-size information, where applicable;
• the call — ruled in, ruled out, or otherwise the explicit decision status.

This documentation rhythm is standing for H1–H4 and is intended to keep the investigation from becoming a set of loose tabs, screenshots, or unsupported narrative. Because this is pre-ruling, the H2 one-pager’s call is deliberately not supplied here.

input.title: Pricing-test change-control checklist
input.body:
# Pricing-test change-control checklist

**Scope:** Applies only to the pricing page under test. It does not restrict changes on other pages or surfaces.

## Blocked on the tested page

- Unrelated layout or UI changes while the pricing test is running.
- Moving, reordering, resizing, collapsing, or otherwise changing page elements outside the approved test treatment.
- Any change that could confound attribution or make the pricing variable harder to isolate.

## Allowed on the tested page

- The approved test treatment and its documented implementation.
- Content or copy changes that do not alter the page layout/UI or the tested variable.
- Measurement, exposure-logging, and instrumentation fixes that are required for a valid read, provided they do not change the page experience.

## Before changing anything

- Confirm whether the change affects layout/UI or the tested variable.
- If it does, defer it until the test ends—or explicitly stop/re-scope the test and document the decision.
- Keep changes on other pages or surfaces governed by their own normal change-control process; this checklist does not block them.

This review must not recast the Q4 shadow work as a launch, Sales queue, pipeline signal, forecast lever, revenue-credit source, or replacement for the simple day-60 nudge. A row that passes the historical evidence gates is **eligible for shadow consideration only**; it does not mean that a live prompt was sent or authorized.

Do not infer account names, evidence, or outcomes that are not present in the source records. Preserve source-row identifiers and record missing or conflicting evidence as `Unknown`, not `Pass`.

## 2. Historical decision standard

A commercial prompt could be considered only when all three readiness signals were present:

- **Deep integration use** — evidence that the account was using integrations beyond a shallow setup.
- **Recent active-admin behavior** — evidence of a currently engaged administrator or qualifying human admin; high activity alone does not substitute for integration depth.
- **Product-visible usage-ceiling evidence** — evidence that product usage was approaching or crossing a visible ceiling.

The three signals were necessary but not sufficient. Apply the following checks before assigning `Eligible for shadow consideration`:

1. **Retained-mid scope:** Confirm that the account was in the retained mid-segment population under review.
2. **CS suppression:** If CS had open adoption, onboarding, import, or similar help work, suppress the commercial prompt. Keep the row in the learning set or false-positive review set where appropriate; do not expose it as a Sales flag.
3. **Renewal-risk suppression:** If the account was in a renewal-risk/save motion, suppress commercial prompting.
4. **Other active-motion collision:** Record an open Sales or CS motion that would make a prompt collide with work already in progress.
5. **Stale or unresolved commercial context:** Do not infer readiness from a stale expansion quote. Hold the row until the quote or other commercial context is rechecked.
6. **Usage-ceiling-only rule:** Usage-ceiling evidence without recent active-admin behavior is insufficient and must be suppressed.
7. **Day-60 boundary:** Where the account was better handled by the simple day-60 nudge and lacked state-model evidence, record that outcome rather than upgrading it to an Expansion Assist commercial state.

## 3. Decision labels

- **Suppress — open CS work:** Open adoption, onboarding, import, or other CS work would make a commercial prompt collide with help already in progress.
- **Suppress — renewal-risk/save motion:** Commercial prompting would be confusing or inappropriate during an active save motion.
- **Suppress — insufficient evidence:** One or more of deep integration, recent active-admin behavior, or product-visible usage-ceiling evidence is absent or unknown.
- **Hold — unresolved quote/context:** A stale expansion quote or other unresolved commercial context prevents interpretation.
- **Keep on simple day-60 path:** The row does not justify replacing the ordinary nudge with the state model.
- **Needs source reconciliation:** The row cannot be decided because the historical source records conflict or are incomplete.

If more than one condition applies, use the strongest blocking condition as the primary disposition and record the others in the rationale. CS suppression takes precedence over a commercial consideration.

requirement.criterion:
The document is a usable audit worksheet for reviewing individual shadow decisions and makes open Customer Success adoption work a suppressing condition: when such work is open, a commercial prompt must not be considered or allowed, regardless of otherwise positive evidence.

The worksheet does not treat usage-ceiling evidence alone as enough for commercial-prompt consideration; it requires active-admin behavior alongside usage-ceiling evidence before a prompt may be considered, without implying that this pair overrides suppression conditions.

input.body:
# Historical chronology — right-ankle running rehabilitation

**Patient:** Riley Tanaka  
**Period covered:** January–April 2027  
**Document status:** Historical record for clinician review, compiled January 1, 2028.

> **Important scope note:** This document describes what was prescribed, completed, and observed during the 2027 rehabilitation period. It is **not current medical clearance**, does not establish present readiness to run, and is not a new progression recommendation. Any present activity decision should be made from a current clinical assessment.

## Clinical context before the restart

- **January 8, 2027 follow-up:** The prior running pause remained in effect after the December 26 focal inside-right-ankle ache during a run-walk session. The documented criteria for a restart were 14 consecutive pain-free days plus a symptom-free 30-minute brisk walk and following-day check. The planned restart was two nonconsecutive 20-minute run-walk sessions per week, alternating four-minute easy runs with one-minute walks. Continuous running was deferred pending six symptom-free run-walk sessions and later clinical review. Ankle-and-calf strengthening was to continue three times weekly.
- **January 23–24:** A 30-minute brisk walk caused no focal ankle pain or gait change during the walk, later that day, or through the following day. The 14-day pain-free requirement was also documented as met.

## Initial run-walk restart: 20-minute sessions

**Structure and safeguards:** Each session used 20 minutes of alternating **four-minute easy running and one-minute walking**. Sessions were kept nonconsecutive, with no third session in a week. The documented stop rule was to stop for focal ankle pain or a gait change. Checks were made during the session, later the same day, and the following day through ordinary walking and stair use. Continuous running remained unapproved during this phase.

- **January 26:** First restart session. Completed the prescribed 20-minute four-minute-run/one-minute-walk pattern. No focal ankle pain, swelling, instability, or gait change during the session or later that day. Ordinary walking and stairs remained symptom-free through **January 27**.
- **January 30:** Second session, kept nonconsecutive from January 26. Same 20-minute interval structure. No focal ankle pain, swelling, instability, or gait change during the intervals or later that day. The planned following-day check was through **January 31**; the subsequent record treated this session as symptom-free.
- **February 2:** Third session, nonconsecutive from the preceding session. Same 20-minute interval structure. No focal ankle pain, swelling, instability, or gait change during the session or later that day. Ordinary walking and stairs remained symptom-free through **February 3**.
- **February 6:** Fourth session. Same four-minute easy-run/one-minute-walk pattern for 20 minutes. The record later grouped this session with the completed symptom-free 20-minute series, including no focal pain, swelling, instability, gait change, or following-day symptoms.
- **February 10:** Fifth session. Same 20-minute interval structure and nonconsecutive spacing. The record later grouped this session with the completed symptom-free series, including no focal pain, swelling, instability, gait change, or following-day symptoms.
- **February 13:** Sixth session. Same 20-minute interval structure and nonconsecutive spacing. The record later grouped this session with the completed symptom-free series, including no focal pain, swelling, instability, gait change, or following-day symptoms.

**Phase result:** By February 13–14, six nonconsecutive 20-minute sessions had been recorded as symptom-free through the session and following-day checks. No third weekly session was added, and continuous running was not treated as authorized before clinical review.

## Interval-progression review and 25-minute run-walk block

- **February 19:** A right-ankle interval-progression review was scheduled after the six clean 20-minute sessions. The record supplied for this chronology does not state the specific examination findings or decision from that visit; the next documented training block was the 25-minute progression below.

**Structure and spacing:** Six nonconsecutive 25-minute sessions used **nine-minute easy runs alternating with one-minute walks**. No third weekly session was added. Ankle-and-calf strengthening continued three times weekly. Each session was assessed during the session, later that day, and the following day.

- **February 21:** 25-minute, nine-minute-run/one-minute-walk intervals; symptom-free during the session, later that day, and the following day.
- **February 24:** Same 25-minute interval structure; symptom-free during the session, later that day, and the following day.
- **February 28:** Same structure; symptom-free during the session, later that day, and the following day.
- **March 3:** Same structure; symptom-free during the session, later that day, and the following day.
- **March 7:** Same structure; symptom-free during the session, later that day, and the following day.
- **March 10:** Same structure; no focal ankle pain, swelling, instability, or gait change during the session or later that day. Ordinary walking and stairs remained symptom-free through **March 11**.

## March clinical transition to continuous running

- **March 15:** Clinical check completed after the six symptom-free 25-minute run-walk sessions. At that time, the documented clearance was for two nonconsecutive 30-minute continuous easy runs per week, while continuing ankle-and-calf strengthening and the session-plus-following-day symptom check. The record specifically did not clear 40-minute runs or a third weekly session.
- **March 17:** First documented 30-minute continuous easy run after the March 15 clinical check. No focal ankle pain, swelling, instability, or gait change during the run or later that day. Ordinary walking and stairs remained symptom-free through **March 18**.
- **March 21:** Second 30-minute continuous easy run, nonconsecutive from March 17. Same symptom findings: no focal ankle pain, swelling, instability, or gait change during the run or later that day; ordinary walking and stairs remained symptom-free through **March 22**.
- **March 24:** 30-minute continuous easy run. No focal ankle pain, swelling, instability, or gait change during the run or later that day. Ordinary walking and stairs remained symptom-free through **March 25**.

## April continuous-run block

**Structure and spacing:** Each documented session was a **30-minute continuous easy run**. The runs remained at two nonconsecutive sessions per week; no third weekly run or 40-minute run was attempted. Ankle-and-calf strengthening continued three times weekly. The session-plus-following-day symptom rule remained in effect.

- **April 4:** 30-minute continuous easy run. No focal ankle pain, swelling, instability, or gait change during the run or later that day. Following-day ordinary walking and stairs remained symptom-free through **April 5**.
- **April 7:** 30-minute continuous easy run, spaced nonconsecutively from April 4. No focal ankle pain, swelling, instability, or gait change during the run or later that day. Following-day ordinary walking and stairs remained symptom-free through **April 8**.
- **April 11:** 30-minute continuous easy run, nonconsecutive from April 7. No focal ankle pain, swelling, instability, or gait change during the run or later that day. Following-day ordinary walking and stairs remained symptom-free through **April 12**.
- **April 14:** 30-minute continuous easy run, nonconsecutive from April 11. No focal ankle pain, swelling, instability, or gait change during the run or later that day. Ordinary walking and stairs remained symptom-free through the **April 15** check.

## Historical summary for clinician review

From the January restart through the April block, the documented progression moved from six 20-minute four-minute-run/one-minute-walk sessions, to six 25-minute nine-minute-run/one-minute-walk sessions, and then—after the March 15 clinical check—to 30-minute continuous easy runs. Sessions were kept nonconsecutive, with no third weekly session. Across the documented sessions, Riley reported no focal ankle pain, swelling, instability, or gait change during the exercise or later the same day, and the recorded following-day checks found ordinary walking and stair use symptom-free. Ankle-and-calf strengthening was continued three times weekly. These statements describe the 2027 record only and should not be interpreted as a current clearance or recommendation.

The record supplied for this chronology does not state the specific examination findings or decision from that visit; the next documented training block was the 25-minute progression below.

**Structure and spacing:** Six nonconsecutive 25-minute sessions used **nine-minute easy runs alternating with one-minute walks**. No third weekly session was added. Ankle-and-calf strengthening continued three times weekly. Each session was assessed during the session, later that day, and the following day.

- **February 21:** 25-minute, nine-minute-run/one-minute-walk intervals; symptom-free during the session, later that day, and the following day.
- **February 24:** Same 25-minute interval structure; symptom-free during the session, later that day, and the following day.
- **February 28:** Same structure; symptom-free during the session, later that day, and the following day.
- **March 3:** Same structure; symptom-free during the session, later that day, and the following day.
- **March 7:** Same structure; symptom-free during the session, later that day, and the following day.
- **March 10:** Same structure; no focal ankle pain, swelling, instability, or gait change during the session or later that day. Ordinary walking and stairs remained symptom-free through **March 11**.

## March clinical transition to continuous running

- **March 15:** Clinical check completed after the six symptom-free 25-minute run-walk sessions. At that time, the documented clearance was for two nonconsecutive 30-minute continuous easy runs per week, while continuing ankle-and-calf strengthening and the session-plus-following-day symptom check. The record specifically did not clear 40-minute runs or a third weekly session.
- **March 17:** First documented 30-minute continuous easy run after the March 15 clinical check. No focal ankle pain, swelling, instability, or gait change during the run or later that day. Ordinary walking and stairs remained symptom-free through **March 18**.
- **March 21:** Second 30-minute continuous easy run, nonconsecutive from March 17. Same symptom findings: no focal ankle pain, swelling, instability, or gait change during the run or later that day; ordinary walking and stairs remained symptom-free through **March 22**.
- **March 24:** 30-minute continuous easy run. No focal ankle pain, swelling, instability, or gait change during the run or later that day. Ordinary walking and stairs remained symptom-free through **March 25**.

## April continuous-run block

**Structure and spacing:** Each documented session was a **30-minute continuous easy run**. The runs remained at two nonconsecutive sessions per week; no third weekly run or 40-minute run was attempted. Ankle-and-calf strengthening continued three times weekly. The session-plus-following-day symptom rule remained in effect.

- **April 7:** 30-minute continuous easy run, spaced nonconsecutively from April 4. No focal ankle pain, swelling, instability, or gait change during the run or later that day. Following-day ordinary walking and stairs remained symptom-free through **April 8**.

input.title: Feb–Apr 2023 Mid-Segment Churn Investigation — H1–H4 Crosswalk
input.body:
# Purpose

Compact crosswalk for the archived investigation documented in **Mid-segment churn investigation Feb-Apr 2023 -- what we learned**. Preserve this numbering when decoding later references.

## Original hypothesis order

- **H1 — Pricing artifact:** Whether packaging, discounting, or contract mix created the apparent churn spike. The concurrent pricing-page experiment was a contamination risk, not a replacement for this hypothesis.
- **H2 — Competitor cycle:** Whether a competitor action or market event caused elevated churn in the mid-segment base.
- **H3 — Onboarding timing:** Whether late-December/early-January starts were maturing into churn on a lag, especially because the day-7 onboarding touch could land at the wrong point relative to activation.
- **H4 — CS coverage gap:** Whether CSM coverage load or coverage drift explained the spike.

## Decoding rule

**H1 = pricing artifact; H2 = competitor cycle; H3 = onboarding timing; H4 = CS coverage gap.** These labels refer to the original hypothesis stack even after the cohort definition moved from the v1 50–200-seat cut to the v2 75–200-seat cut.

observed.body:
# Purpose

Compact crosswalk for the archived investigation documented in **Mid-segment churn investigation Feb-Apr 2023 -- what we learned**. Preserve this numbering when decoding later references.

## Original hypothesis order

- **H1 — Pricing artifact:** Whether packaging, discounting, or contract mix created the apparent churn spike. The concurrent pricing-page experiment was a contamination risk, not a replacement for this hypothesis.
- **H2 — Competitor cycle:** Whether a competitor action or market event caused elevated churn in the mid-segment base.
- **H3 — Onboarding timing:** Whether late-December/early-January starts were maturing into churn on a lag, especially because the day-7 onboarding touch could land at the wrong point relative to activation.
- **H4 — CS coverage gap:** Whether CSM coverage load or coverage drift explained the spike.

## Decoding rule

**H1 = pricing artifact; H2 = competitor cycle; H3 = onboarding timing; H4 = CS coverage gap.** These labels refer to the original hypothesis stack even after the cohort definition moved from the v1 50–200-seat cut to the v2 75–200-seat cut.

checks.reason: The body presents an ordered H1–H4 bullet crosswalk and explicitly states: “H1 = pricing artifact; H2 = competitor cycle; H3 = onboarding timing; H4 = CS coverage gap.”

tests.request: The pricing-page experiment archive needs a card that records what EXP-2023-02-pricing-page's original treatment was intended to prove before the later result is discussed. Create the historical design-hypothesis card with the treatment concept, target customer tiers, intended conversion outcome, and minimum lift, clearly labeling all of it as the original design hypothesis rather than an observed result.

input.title: EXP-2023-02-pricing-page — Historical Design-Hypothesis Card
input.body:
# Historical design hypothesis

**Status:** Original design hypothesis only — not an observed result.

## Treatment concept
The proposed treatment simplified the pricing-page layout and made the value-per-seat framing explicit, with the goal of reducing visual clutter and clarifying packaging for prospective customers.

## Target customer tiers
The hypothesis focused on self-serve conversion in the **Starter** and **Growth** tiers.

## Intended conversion outcome
The treatment was intended to increase Starter/Growth conversion, particularly by improving the rate at which pricing-page visitors progressed into checkout and ultimately converted to paid customers.

## Minimum lift
The minimum intended improvement was **at least +1.5 percentage points** in Starter/Growth conversion.

> This card records what the experiment was designed to prove before any readout. It must not be interpreted as evidence that the treatment achieved the stated outcome or lift.

input.title: Helio Start change-sequencing checklist
input.body:
# Helio Start change-sequencing checklist

Use this as a gate order, not as a launch or revenue plan. A downstream item stays blocked until the prerequisite is explicitly settled and the measurement path is clean.

## Core sequence

1. **Eligibility and refusal rules → packaging**
2. **Event taxonomy and entitlement state → pricing-page experiment**
3. **Lifecycle fork and support-routing boundaries → paid acquisition**
4. **Measurement spine and population definitions → activation measurement and interpretation**

## Checklist

### 1. Packaging

- [ ] **Settle eligibility and refusal rules first.** Define the under-50 self-serve shape, deployment simplicity, verified admin ownership, supported billing, connector/access requirements, and external-authority constraints. Explicitly route manual billing, migration/import help, unsupported permissions, unclear ownership, and other assisted/refusal cases out of the self-serve path.
- [ ] **Make the admission state operational.** The rules must distinguish self-serve-eligible accounts from sales- or CS-assisted accounts; seat count alone is not sufficient.
- **Blocks:** packaging and offer promises, customer-facing positioning, eligibility-dependent entitlement design, and any public framing that implies broader availability than the refusal rules support.

### 2. Pricing-page experiment

- [ ] **Settle clean event taxonomy and entitlement instrumentation first.** At minimum, the path must capture admin-complexity signal, `first_integration_connected`, import or migration help, support handoff, billing exceptions, and `entitlement_state` without inferring eligibility from a plan name.
- [ ] **Verify the instrumentation path.** Billing must sign off; the entitlement path must be QA-clean; backfills and state transitions must be documented; and events must distinguish self-serve-eligible accounts from sales- or CS-assisted accounts.
- [ ] **Hold the experiment design clean.** Do not run it concurrently with an unrelated pricing-page layout or UI change. Design exploration may continue, but experiment execution and public exposure wait for the gate.
- **Blocks:** running a pricing-page experiment, interpreting experiment results, public pricing-page copy or exposure, and any launch claim based on an unclean measurement path.

### 3. Paid acquisition

- [ ] **Settle the lifecycle fork first.** Define which path is self-serve education, which cases require assisted support, and which state-changing lifecycle touches remain prohibited. Keep suppression and eligibility behavior intact; do not create a paid-source bypass.
- [ ] **Settle support-load and unsupported-admission guardrails.** Account-level support effort, assisted-route reasons, and unsupported cases entering admission must be observable from first contact. Support load remains a first-class outcome beside activation.
- [ ] **Reconfirm the product and evidence boundaries.** Preserve eligibility, refusal, connector-access, external-authority, instrumentation, and support-routing rules. Any paid test also requires its own budget and acquisition authorization; proposal preparation is not approval to run traffic.
- **Blocks:** paid traffic, paid-source audience expansion, paid-acquisition success claims, pipeline targets, and forecast credit. Organic activation or first-paid evidence alone does not authorize a paid test or establish unit economics.

### 4. Activation measurement

- [ ] **Settle the measurement contract first.** Use the approved activation definition, including what counts as a real first integration; exclude misleading proxy events such as template-only setup where applicable. Define denominators, cohort windows, admission status, and treatment of incomplete or assisted cases.
- [ ] **Settle population boundaries before reporting.** Keep Helio Start activation and support-load reporting separate from retained mid-segment reporting. Use activation definition v3 for Helio Start, keep the 75–200-seat retained mid-seg on v2, and show the 50–75-seat band separately.
- [ ] **Keep eligibility and deployment shape visible.** Measurement tables must identify sub-50 seats, deployment shape, and eligibility/refusal status rather than collapsing all workspaces into one rate.
- [ ] **Read support load beside activation.** Activation is not sufficient by itself; include support load, permissions, imports, billing expectations, migration complexity, and routed-before-setup cases in the interpretation.
- **Blocks:** activation dashboards, cohort comparisons, beta or exposure decisions, lifecycle optimization based on the read, and any leap from observed activation or first payment to durable retention, paid-acquisition readiness, pipeline, or forecastable revenue.

## Standing boundaries

- [ ] Do not imply pricing-page exposure before eligibility, instrumentation, lifecycle, and support gates are clean.
- [ ] Do not merge Helio Start with retained mid-seg, Expansion Assist, or other populations to improve an activation read.
- [ ] Keep design exploration distinct from experiment execution: exploration can proceed while a pricing-page experiment remains blocked.
- [ ] Preserve refusal and assisted routing; do not treat a successful activation signal as evidence that excluded cases are eligible.
- [ ] Treat any paid-acquisition proposal, budget, traffic, pipeline, or forecast decision as a separate approval, not as an automatic consequence of clearing the earlier gates.
